statement: What happens after MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD ends is known from the sponsor's phase 2 programme only through two follow-ups without a comparison group. In the first US trial, 16 of the 19 people treated with MDMA were reassessed 17 to 74 months (mean about 45) after their last MDMA session: their mean CAPS score was similar to that 2 months after their second MDMA session (23.7 against 24.6; mean change −0.9 points, 95% CI −17.6 to 15.9, editors' calculation), but individual scores moved widely in both directions; 2 of the 16 scored above the trial's entry threshold again, which the authors count as relapse; 3 of the 19 were not reassessed; and at follow-up 8 of 19 were in psychotherapy and 12 of 19 took psychiatric medicines. On a questionnaire written by the investigators, all 19 reported some benefit and none reported harm from taking part; 8 reported some cannabis use and 1 psilocybin use, all of whom had used these before the trial, and 1 reported using ecstasy once (Mithoefer et al., 2013). In pooled open-label data from four other phase 2 trials, corrected after an ethical violation by two therapists at one site and under an expression of concern, mean CAPS-IV scores 12 months after treatment were lower than at the end of treatment (35.3 against 42.5 on a 0 to 136 scale; 58 participants), by which time everyone had received full-dose MDMA (Ponte et al., 2021, and its correction, 2025). The sponsor's pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials (Jerome et al., 2020) is among the retracted papers described in this section and is not used; the follow-up of the phase 3 trials is the subject of a separate claim in this section. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In one small early trial, 16 of 19 people were checked again about 4 years later. On average their PTSD scores were about the same as soon after treatment, but some people got much better and some much worse, and 2 had moderate-to-severe PTSD again. Many were also getting other therapy or medicines, and there was no comparison group. In four other early trials, scores a year later were a little lower than at the end of treatment, again with no comparison group, and the results had to be corrected after an ethics breach by two therapists at one site.
population: Adults with chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD treated with MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in the sponsor's phase 2 trials (first US trial, 19 treated with MDMA; four later trials pooled, 59 after the correction)
exposure: Two or three MDMA sessions within manualized psychotherapy (randomized stage or open-label crossover)
comparator: None at follow-up: the same participants' scores at the end of treatment
outcome: PTSD symptom severity (CAPS-IV) 12 months and 17 to 74 months after treatment; relapse (CAPS above 50); later psychotherapy and psychiatric medicines; self-reported benefit, harm and drug use during follow-up
magnitude: First US trial (Mithoefer 2013): CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) 2 months after the second MDMA session and 23.7 (22.8) at follow-up, n = 16, matched t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; editors' calculation from Table 2: mean change −0.9 (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9), SD of individual changes 31.4, 6 of 16 improved and 3 worsened by 10 points or more; CAPS above 50 in 2 of 16 (13%), or 5 of 19 (26%) counting the 3 not reassessed as negative outcomes; at follow-up 8 of 19 in psychotherapy (16 of 19 at enrolment) and 12 of 19 on psychiatric medicines (12 of 19 at entry). Questionnaire: 19 of 19 some benefit, 0 of 19 harm; cannabis 8, psilocybin 1 (all with earlier use), ecstasy once 1. Four pooled phase 2 trials, corrected (Ponte 2021; correction 2025): CAPS-IV least-squares means 88.22 at baseline, 42.46 at treatment exit and 35.28 at 12 months; treatment exit to 12 months −7.18 (SE 2.60), p = .008, N = 58.

evidence.locator: Methods and materials › Subjects, 1st to 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Original trial: 20 randomized (12 MDMA, 8 placebo with the same psychotherapy); 7 of 8 placebo participants crossed over to open-label MDMA, so 19 were treated with MDMA; follow-up added by protocol amendment; CAPS and IES-R completed by 16 of the 19 (one lost after moving, two declined, one of them having had the smallest earlier response and fearing symptoms would be triggered); CAPS 17 to 74 months after the final MDMA session (mean 45.4, SD 17.3, n = 17).

evidence.locator: Results › CAPS and IES-R, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
evidence.extracted: CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) at 2 months and 23.7 (22.8) at follow-up, t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; IES-R 19.8 (19.5) and 22.1 (21.8), p = 0.72; 2 of 16 completers (13%) above 50 at follow-up, the cut-off for entry to the original study, which the authors call relapse to moderate-to-severe PTSD; counting the 3 non-completers as negative outcomes too, 5 of 19 (26%).

evidence.locator: Table 2 (editors' calculation)
evidence.extracted: Editors' calculation from the 16 completers' individual scores, which reproduce Table 1's means and SDs: mean change from 2 months to follow-up −0.9 points (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9, paired t −0.11), SD of individual changes 31.4; 6 improved by 10 points or more and 3 worsened by 10 points or more (the two relapses from 16 to 60 and from 6 to 91). For the 8 participants who later had a third MDMA session, the 2-month score was taken before it.

evidence.locator: Results › Participation in psychotherapy; Results › Psychiatric medications; Table 4; Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: In psychotherapy at enrolment 16 of 19, at follow-up 8 of 19; on psychiatric medicines 12 of 19 at entry and at follow-up. The authors state there was no meaningful control group at follow-up, that natural history or uncontrolled variables could explain the results, and that later psychotherapy and medicines are the most important confounder and preclude a definite conclusion about long-term benefit.

evidence.locator: Results › LTFU questionnaire results for 19 PTSD subjects › Degree of benefit, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Results › Questions about illicit drug use during LTFU period
evidence.extracted: On the investigators' own follow-up questionnaire, all 19 MDMA-treated participants reported some benefit and none reported harm from taking part; cannabis use by 8 (once to occasionally) and psilocybin mushrooms by 1, all of whom reported use before enrolment; 1 participant reported using ecstasy once, in an attempt at a therapeutic setting, and found it unsatisfactory.

evidence.locator: Methods and materials › Study design, 2nd paragraph; Footnotes › Conflict of interest
evidence.extracted: The follow-up CAPS was administered in person or by phone by the same independent rater as in the original trial; the sponsor paid this rater, who is the second author, and played a role in the study design, data analysis and writing.

evidence.locator: Corrected Table 3; Summary of corrections made › Open-label endpoints, 1st paragraph (revised text)
evidence.extracted: Corrected open-label analysis of the four pooled trials (N = 58): CAPS-IV least-squares means 88.22 at baseline, 42.46 at treatment exit and 35.28 at 12-month follow-up; treatment exit to 12 months −7.18 (SE 2.60), p = .008.

evidence.locator: Results › Open-Label Endpoints: Treatment Exit and Long-Term Follow-Up, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 note; Method › Measures › PTSD Symptoms, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: After the blinded endpoint, all participants received full-dose MDMA in open-label sessions; groups were pooled for treatment exit and the 12-month follow-up, which took place after the final open-label session, so these comparisons are within-person and uncontrolled. CAPS-IV total severity scores range from 0 to 136.

evidence.locator: Notice, 2nd to 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Expression of concern (3 December 2024): an ethical violation by a pair of therapists who treated 4 of the 6 MP-4 participants caused a protocol deviation; the authors had not told the journal at submission in December 2019, although the violation was publicly announced in May 2019; the data of those therapists are removed by correction; the journal judged the non-disclosure improper and its investigation of human-subjects ethics inconclusive.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Jerome 2020 row)
evidence.extracted: Across the studies reviewed to October 2023, conclusions were possible only for acute and short-term side effects, because insufficient data were available on longer-term risks beyond active treatment; the one included study that formally assessed long-term follow-up outcomes was the pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials by Jerome et al. (2020), which the PMC reference list now marks as retracted.

evidence.locator: Conclusion, 7th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Among the review's research priorities: longer follow-ups in clinical trials, because short-term outcomes, positive and negative, often change in the weeks and months after a typical trial ends.

risk_of_bias.note: Uncontrolled follow-ups with unblinded outcome assessment (in the first trial by a co-author paid by the sponsor), 16% not reassessed, co-treatment in most participants, an unvalidated questionnaire, and, for the pooled data, an expression of concern and analysis choices made after inspecting outcomes.

imprecision.note: 16 participants in the long follow-up; the 95% interval for the mean change runs from a 17.6-point improvement to a 15.9-point worsening.

publication_bias.note: Not rated down, but the programme's other long follow-up is retracted, so the published record is thin.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim about what was observed after treatment in two cohorts without comparison groups (METHODS §6.3: descriptive claims start low). Rated down once for risk of bias (unblinded and partly sponsor-paid assessment, missing data, co-treatment, an unvalidated questionnaire, an expression of concern on the pooled data) and once for imprecision (16 people in the long follow-up, with an interval compatible with large improvement or large worsening). The claim does not say that the benefit lasted because of MDMA: neither follow-up can separate the treatment's effect from later therapy, medicines or the natural course. Both follow-ups come from the same sponsor's phase 2 programme and share investigators, so their agreement is not independent replication.

statement: In the sponsor's pooled analysis of four phase 2 trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for chronic PTSD, as corrected (correction published online in December 2024: four participants of one site, treated by two therapists involved in an ethical violation, were removed, and the journal issued an expression of concern because the authors had not disclosed the violation at submission), full-dose MDMA compared with low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy was associated with a larger improvement in self-reported sleep quality 1 to 2 months after two blinded sessions: change on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (0 to 21, higher is worse) −3.5 against +0.5 points (Hedges' g 0.85, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.47; 44 and 14 participants), with an improvement of at least 3 points in 24 of 45 against 2 of 14. After open-label full-dose treatment for everyone, mean scores 12 months later were about 1 point lower than at the end of treatment (7.1 against 8.2), without a comparison group. The paper reports no check of whether participants could tell their dose, the outcome is self-reported, the analyses were not preregistered and the dose groups were defined partly after inspecting outcomes. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In four early trials run for the same sponsor, people with PTSD who had full doses of MDMA said they slept better a month or two later than people who had a very small dose: about 4 points better on a 0 to 21 sleep scale. A year later their sleep was a little better still, but by then everyone had had full doses, so there was nothing to compare with. No one checked whether people could tell which dose they had, and the results had to be corrected after an ethics breach at one site.
population: Adults with chronic PTSD in four of the sponsor's phase 2 trials (59 after the correction: 45 full dose, 14 low dose)
exposure: Two blinded sessions with full-dose MDMA within manualized psychotherapy
comparator: Low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy (no inactive placebo after the correction)
outcome: Change in self-reported sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) from baseline to 1 to 2 months after the blinded sessions; open-label change to 12 months
magnitude: Corrected blinded endpoint: PSQI change −3.51 (SD 5.08, n = 44) against +0.50 (3.25, n = 14), p = .008, Hedges' g 0.85 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.47); improvement of 3 points or more in 24 of 45 (53.3%) against 2 of 14 (14.3%). Corrected open-label, N = 58: PSQI least-squares means 12.59 at baseline, 8.18 at treatment exit, 7.09 at 12 months; exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029. Original (superseded) analysis: −3.53 against +0.56, g 0.88, p = .003.

evidence.locator: Results › Blinded Endpoint, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Original analysis, superseded by the correction: PSQI change −3.53 (SD 5.03) in the active group against +0.56 (3.05) in the control group (n = 16; active n printed as 46 in Table 2 and 47 elsewhere), p = .003, Hedges' g 0.88 with a printed 95% CI of −0.27 to 2.03 that does not fit g; a drop of 3 points or more in 53.2% against 12.5% (N = 61).

evidence.locator: Summary of corrections made › Blinded endpoint, 1st paragraph (revised text); corrected Table 2
evidence.extracted: Corrected blinded endpoint: PSQI change −3.51 (SD 5.08) in the active group (n = 44) against +0.50 (3.25) in the control group (n = 14), p = .008, Hedges' g 0.85 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.47); CAPS-IV −34.93 against −11.07, g 0.96 (0.33 to 1.59).

evidence.locator: Corrected Table 2, note b
evidence.extracted: PSQI fell by 3 points or more in 24 active participants (53.3%, of 45) and 2 controls (14.3%, of 14), p = .008; the footnote's counts and denominators do not fully agree (19 active without such a drop, n = 44 in the table).

evidence.locator: Corrected Table 3
evidence.extracted: Open-label (N = 58): PSQI least-squares means 12.59 at baseline, 8.18 at treatment exit, 7.09 at 12 months; change from exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029.

evidence.locator: Description and explanation for this correction; Summary of corrections made › In the abstract
evidence.extracted: The four MP-4 participants treated by the pair of therapists were removed; sample 63 to 59 (active 47 to 45, control 16 to 14); the removed participants were the only ones in the control group given no MDMA, so the control group now consists only of low-dose MDMA and the placebo label is dropped.

evidence.locator: Notice, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors had not notified the journal of the ethical violation at submission (December 2019), although it had been publicly announced in May 2019; the journal judged this improper and issued the expression of concern; its investigation of human-subjects ethics was inconclusive.

evidence.locator: Method › Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Open Practices Statement
evidence.extracted: Doses pooled into control and active groups by the protocols' designations and by inspection of post-treatment CAPS-IV scores (citing the since-retracted pooled analysis by Mithoefer et al., 2019); independent-samples t tests; no power analysis; the analyses were not formally preregistered.

evidence.locator: Method › Measures › Sleep Quality, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Sleep quality was measured with the self-report PSQI (global score 0 to 21; a cut-off of 5 separates good from poor sleepers); the authors list the small, mostly White sample and self-reported outcomes as limitations; the paper reports no assessment of whether participants could tell their dose.

risk_of_bias.note: Very serious: self-reported outcome without any check of blinding; analysis not preregistered, with groups defined partly after inspecting outcomes and pooled without stratification; the data were corrected after an ethical violation at one site, under an expression of concern.

imprecision.note: 58 participants, 14 controls; the interval for g runs from 0.23 to 1.47.

grade.reasoning: The blinded comparison rests on randomization within each trial, so it starts high, but it is rated down twice for risk of bias (RoB 2 high on the study card: a self-reported outcome with no check of blinding, outcome-informed grouping, unstratified pooling, no preregistration, and the expression of concern) and once for imprecision. The relation is an association rather than a causal verb because the pooled comparison does not preserve each trial's randomization. The 12-month figures are uncontrolled and are given only as a description. This is one pooled analysis whose per-trial results are not reported, hence single study.

verification.flag_note: Not in the brief's list of suggested ids; proposed because the assignment included this analysis and its expression of concern. statement: In the clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy reviewed up to 2024, almost all in PTSD (outside PTSD, one randomized trial each in 12 autistic adults with social anxiety and in 18 people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, plus small open-label studies and a case series), MDMA compared with placebo or low-dose MDMA increased common side effects during sessions and in the following week, such as jaw clenching or muscle tightness, anxiety, reduced appetite, nausea, sweating, feeling cold and headache, which the reviews describe as mostly mild to moderate and largely transient. A 2024 meta-analysis found higher odds of any expected reaction during sessions in phase 2 trials (odds ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.49) and of any treatment-emergent adverse event in the two phase 3 trials (3.51, 2.76 to 4.46), although its any-event percentages cannot be shares of participants; in the life-threatening-illness trial, jaw clenching occurred in 11 of 13 people on MDMA and 1 of 5 on placebo. The meta-analysis found no difference in psychiatric adverse events (phase 2), in suicidality or cardiac events of special interest (phase 3) or in dropping out, and a network meta-analysis found no excess of severe adverse events; a 2022 review found one serious adverse event related to MDMA in the studies it covered (more frequent premature heartbeats, present before treatment, needing a night of hospital monitoring). The record of harms is weak: most studies relied on spontaneous reports, no trial reported harms adequately by the CONSORT Harms 2022 standard, 56% of the non-serious and 4 of the 13 serious adverse events listed in the trial registries were missing from the publications (the 4 all in MDMA groups), and the meta-analysis found too little data on risks beyond active treatment, from small and highly selected samples. Certainty: low (for the increase in common side effects). Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In trials, mostly for PTSD, MDMA often caused side effects such as a tight jaw, tight muscles, worry, less appetite, feeling sick, sweating or feeling cold. These were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose, and they mostly passed within a week. Few serious problems were recorded, but many trials only noted problems people mentioned themselves, some recorded problems never made it into the published papers, and there is too little information on what happens later.
population: People treated in clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy: mostly adults with PTSD; also autistic adults with social anxiety, people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, people with alcohol use disorder (open-label) and couples in which one partner has PTSD
exposure: MDMA in one to three sessions within psychotherapy
comparator: Inactive placebo or low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy
outcome: Side effects and adverse events during and after treatment, serious adverse events, adverse events of special interest, withdrawal, and completeness of harms reporting
magnitude: Colcott 2024 (8 randomized trials, 298 participants, in the meta-analyses; 13 studies, 333 participants, in the review): phase 2, any expected reaction during sessions OR 1.67 (1.12 to 2.49), 45% against 30%; in the following 7 days OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), 46% against 31%; anxiety OR 4.7 and jaw clenching OR 4.8 during sessions; phase 3, any TEAE OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), 16% against 5% (unit unclear), 13 named TEAEs more frequent; no difference in phase 2 TEAEs or psychiatric TEAEs, phase 3 suicidality or cardiac AESIs, or withdrawal. Registers against publications: 1487 against 661 non-serious events (5 trials), 13 against 9 serious events (8 trials). Life-threatening illness trial (Schipper 2024, Table 4): jaw clenching 11/13 (84.6%) against 1/5 (20.0%), thirst 11/13 against 2/5, perspiration 9/13 against 0/5; no treatment-related serious adverse events. Autistic adults (Breeksema 2022, Table 1): acute anxiety 6/8 against 1/4.

evidence.locator: Results › Study selection, 1st paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 13 studies with 333 unique participants; 8 randomized trials (298 participants) in the meta-analyses: seven in PTSD and one in autistic adults with social anxiety (Danforth 2018, 12); non-randomized studies in PTSD, couples with one partner with PTSD, alcohol use disorder (14) and a Swiss case series.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Results › Systematic review: reporting of side effects, 1st paragraph; Results › Phase two studies, side effects during and 7 days following medication sessions; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Phase 2 side effects were the protocols' spontaneously reported reactions, a subset of adverse events expected from studies in healthy volunteers, recorded during and for 7 days after sessions. Any such reaction during sessions OR 1.67 (95% CI 1.12 to 2.49), 45% against 30%; in the 7 days after OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), 46% against 31%; anxiety (OR 4.7) and jaw clenching (OR 4.8) during sessions more likely with MDMA; the review describes the side effects as largely transient and mild or moderate in severity.

evidence.locator: Results › Phase three studies › Treatment emergent adverse events, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Phase 3: any treatment-emergent adverse event OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), 16% against 5%; more likely with MDMA: muscle tightness, decreased appetite, nausea, excessive perspiration, feeling cold, restlessness, dilated pupils, jaw clenching or tight jaw, uncontrolled eye movements, feeling jittery, non-cardiac chest pain or discomfort, blurred vision, chills.

evidence.locator: Results › Phase three studies › Treatment emergent adverse events, 1st paragraph, against Table 1 (Mitchell 2021 and 2023 rows) (editors' comparison)
evidence.extracted: The any-event proportions cannot be shares of participants: 16% of MDMA participants with any TEAE in phase 3, while Table 1 lists muscle tightness alone in 63% and 58.5% of the MDMA arms; the unit of analysis is not stated, so the pooled any-event odds ratios indicate direction only.

evidence.locator: Results › Phase two studies › Treatment emergent adverse events (TEAE); Phase three studies › Adverse event of special interest (AESI); Phase 2 and 3 studies › Withdrawal
evidence.extracted: No difference in any TEAE or psychiatric TEAE in phase 2 (lower odds of TEAEs with MDMA in the PTSD subgroup, two studies with low-dose controls); no difference in suicidality or cardiac adverse events of special interest in phase 3 and no events of abuse, misuse or diversion reported; no difference in withdrawal.

evidence.locator: Results › Comparison of adverse events published versus reported on ClinicalTrial.gov; Results › Adherence to CONSORT Harms 2022; Results › Risk of bias, 1st paragraph; Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Registers listed 1487 non-serious adverse events against 661 in the articles (5 trials) and 13 serious events against 9 (8 trials); the 4 unpublished serious events were in MDMA groups (CNS metastases, clavicle fracture, syncope, suicidal behaviour); no trial reached adequate CONSORT Harms 2022 adherence (median 50%, range 21% to 64%); 7 of 8 trials at high risk of bias for side effects; 11 of 13 studies used passive monitoring.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Conclusions only for acute and short-term side effects, with insufficient data on longer-term risks beyond active treatment; a limited number of studies with highly selective samples, largely small studies sponsored by a single advocacy group; side effects likely to be more frequent outside controlled trials.

evidence.locator: Table 4 (adverse events), Wolfson 2020 rows; Table 3 (serious and grade 3/4 events); Results › Effects of interventions › Entactogens (MDMA) › Secondary outcomes, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Life-threatening illness trial (13 MDMA, 5 placebo): jaw clenching 11 (84.6%) against 1 (20.0%), thirst 11 (84.6%) against 2 (40.0%), dry mouth 9 (69.2%) against 1 (20.0%), perspiration 9 (69.2%) against 0, headache 8 (61.5%) against 1 (20.0%); no treatment-related serious or grade 3 or 4 adverse events; the reactions were short and mostly resolved by the end of the session or during the following week.

evidence.locator: Table 1, Danforth et al. (2018) row; Results › MDMA › Adverse events › Social anxiety
evidence.extracted: Autistic adults with social anxiety (8 MDMA, 4 placebo): acute anxiety 6 (75%) against 1 (25%), difficulty concentrating 5 (63%) against 1 (25%); 2 of 8 on MDMA and 1 of 4 on placebo reported depressed mood, suicidal ideation and panic attack after the first session; no serious adverse events.

evidence.locator: Results › MDMA › Physiological effects; Results › MDMA › Quality appraisal
evidence.extracted: Nine MDMA studies reported mild, transient rises in blood pressure, temperature and heart rate during sessions, none needing intervention; one MDMA-related serious adverse event (more frequent premature ventricular contractions, present at baseline, one night of hospital monitoring, resolved; Mithoefer 2018); 11 MDMA studies recorded adverse events only when spontaneously reported.

evidence.locator: Results › All cause discontinuation and severe adverse event
evidence.extracted: In the network meta-analysis of depressive symptoms, no intervention, MDMA included, was associated with more all-cause discontinuation or severe adverse events than the placebo arms of psychedelic trials.

risk_of_bias.note: Side effects mostly recorded from spontaneous reports by staff who probably knew the allocation; 7 of 8 trials at high risk of bias for this outcome.

indirectness.note: The claim covers trials across indications, but the evidence comes mostly from PTSD trials of one sponsor's protocol and is seen through systematic reviews.

imprecision.note: Not rated down for the common effects, whose differences are large and consistent at trial level; the pooled any-event intervals are probably too narrow and are not relied on.

publication_bias.note: Registered adverse events missing from publications would bias towards fewer reported harms, not create the observed increase; stated in the claim rather than rated down.

grade.reasoning: Randomized comparisons start high. Rated down once for risk of bias (spontaneous, probably unblinded recording) and once for indirectness (a claim across indications resting mostly on PTSD trials of one sponsor, seen through systematic reviews). Certainty applies to the increase in common side effects; rare, serious or delayed harms cannot be assessed from these trials, which the claim says. The causal verb is used because the comparisons are randomized and the effects are those expected pharmacologically, although the reviews themselves describe them as associations. Most trials share the sponsor and protocol, hence replicated by the same team. This overlaps the phase 3 adverse-event claim in this section, which rests on the trial reports read directly.

statement: For conditions other than PTSD, evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA-assisted therapy helps. The systematic reviews read here (searches up to March 2024) found only small studies outside PTSD: one randomized trial each in anxiety related to a life-threatening illness (18 people), social anxiety in autistic adults (12) and tinnitus (13), an open-label study in alcohol use disorder (14), an uncontrolled study of couples in which one partner has PTSD (6 couples) and a Swiss case series. The Cochrane review rated the evidence in life-threatening illness very uncertain: in its one trial, MDMA against placebo changed trait anxiety by −14.7 points on a 20 to 80 scale (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05) and depression by −6.3 points on a 0 to 63 scale (−16.93 to 4.33). A network meta-analysis of depressive symptoms, whose MDMA trials were mostly in PTSD, found high-dose MDMA better than the placebo arms of psychedelic trials by 5.3 HAMD-17 points (95% credible interval 2.26 to 8.32) but not clearly better than the placebo arms of antidepressant trials (1.5, −2.79 to 5.78), a comparison made only indirectly. A critical narrative review found that, for MDMA, only the two phase 3 PTSD trials met its minimum standard (randomized, more than 15 people per group) and called MDMA for PTSD a signal needing replication. The reviews report that blinding was rarely achieved and that controlled follow-up was short. Certainty: very low. Status: single study (one trial per condition outside PTSD).
plain: The reviews up to 2024 found only a few very small studies of MDMA therapy outside PTSD: in people anxious about a life-threatening illness, autistic adults with social anxiety, people with tinnitus, people with alcohol problems and couples. Each had one small trial or no comparison group at all. The best review says the results for serious illness are very uncertain. So nobody can yet say whether MDMA therapy helps any of these conditions.
population: People with conditions other than PTSD: anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, social anxiety in autistic adults, tinnitus, alcohol use disorder, couples with one partner with PTSD, depressive symptoms
exposure: MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA in one to three sessions with psychotherapy)
comparator: Placebo or low-dose MDMA with the same therapy; none in open-label and uncontrolled studies
outcome: Condition-specific symptoms (anxiety, depression); number and design of the trials available

statement: As analysed by a Cochrane review, in adults with anxiety related to a life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness (one randomized trial, 18 people: 13 on MDMA, 5 on placebo), evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA given in two sessions within psychotherapy, compared with a lactose placebo with the same therapy, reduces anxiety or depression: 1 month after the second session the differences were −14.7 points in trait anxiety on a 20 to 80 scale (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05), −16.1 in state anxiety (−33.03 to 0.83) and −6.3 in depression on a 0 to 63 scale (−16.93 to 4.33), intervals the review computed conservatively; global functioning and quality of life did not differ clearly. There were no treatment-related serious adverse events, while jaw clenching (11 of 13 against 1 of 5) and other side effects, mostly resolved within a week, were common on MDMA. More than 80% of participants and investigators guessed the allocation, and outcomes measured more than 3 months later have no comparison group, because the placebo group had by then crossed over to MDMA. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: One small trial, as analysed in a Cochrane review, gave MDMA or a dummy pill with talking therapy to 18 people anxious about a life-threatening illness. Anxiety scores fell more with MDMA, but the trial was too small to be sure the difference was real. MDMA often caused a tight jaw and other side effects that mostly passed within a week, and no serious harms were linked to it. Most people could tell which pill they had.
population: Adults with anxiety (STAI-Trait above 45) related to a life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness, life expectancy of at least 9 months (one trial, 18 randomized: 13 MDMA, 5 placebo)
exposure: MDMA in two blinded sessions within nine non-drug psychotherapy sessions
comparator: Lactose placebo with the same psychotherapy
outcome: Trait and state anxiety (STAI), depression (BDI-II), global functioning and quality of life 1 month after the second session; serious and common adverse events
magnitude: STAI-T mean difference −14.70 (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05); STAI-S −16.10 (−33.03 to 0.83); BDI-II −6.30 (−16.93 to 4.33); GAF 75.1 against 72.8 at 1 month (p = 0.52); FACIT subscales p 0.15 to 0.87; computed from change scores assuming no pre-post correlation (wider intervals). Adverse events: jaw clenching 11/13 against 1/5, thirst 11/13 against 2/5, perspiration 9/13 against 0/5; no treatment-related serious or grade 3 or 4 events.

statement: In a network meta-analysis of randomized trials reporting depressive symptoms (searched to 12 October 2023), whose MDMA trials enrolled mostly people with PTSD, high-dose MDMA-assisted therapy was associated with a larger reduction in depressive symptoms than the placebo arms of psychedelic trials, by 5.3 points on the HAMD-17 (95% credible interval 2.26 to 8.32), but evidence is insufficient to say whether it does better than the placebo arms of antidepressant trials, which themselves did better than those of psychedelic trials (1.5 points, −2.79 to 5.78, a comparison made only indirectly, through one psilocybin trial and across different diagnoses); against extremely low-dose psilocybin the difference was 1.4 (−3.08 to 5.84), and high-dose psilocybin did better than high-dose MDMA (5.0, 1.23 to 8.67). No intervention had more severe adverse events or dropouts than the psychedelic trials' placebo arms. The MDMA estimates concern depressive symptoms in trials of other conditions, not depression as the main diagnosis, and only acute outcomes. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: A big review compared several treatments for low mood. In MDMA trials, mostly done in people with PTSD, low mood improved more with MDMA than with a dummy pill: about 5 points on a common depression scale. But when the review compared MDMA, in a roundabout way, with how people do on a dummy pill in antidepressant trials, the difference was small and could be zero. These trials were not done in people whose main problem was depression.
population: Adults in randomized trials with depressive symptoms as an outcome; the MDMA trials enrolled mostly people with PTSD
exposure: High-dose MDMA (as the review defines it) within psychotherapy
comparator: Placebo arms of psychedelic trials; placebo arms of escitalopram trials (indirect); extremely low-dose psilocybin (indirect)
outcome: Change in depressive symptoms (HAMD-17 or converted scales) at the end of treatment; all-cause discontinuation; severe adverse events
magnitude: High-dose MDMA: 5.32 HAMD-17 points (95% CrI 2.26 to 8.32; SMD 0.42) against psychedelic-trial placebo; 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78; SMD 0.08) against antidepressant-trial placebo; 1.36 (−3.08 to 5.84) against extremely low-dose psilocybin. Low-dose MDMA against psychedelic-trial placebo 4.92 (−0.26 to 9.94). Antidepressant-trial placebo against psychedelic-trial placebo 3.79 (0.77 to 6.80). High-dose psilocybin against high-dose MDMA 4.98 (1.23 to 8.67). The review's minimal important difference: 3 points.

evidence.extracted: Searched from database inception to 12 October 2023; psychedelics were compared with the placebo arms of psychedelic trials and escitalopram with those of antidepressant trials, the two parts joined by one head-to-head psilocybin-escitalopram trial; participants in the MDMA trials were predominantly diagnosed with PTSD, those in the escitalopram trials with major depressive disorder; only acute effects were extracted.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials in a network, starting high; rated down once each for risk of bias (unblinding), indirectness (PTSD populations; indirect comparison through one psilocybin trial) and imprecision. The claim states insufficient evidence for a benefit beyond what placebo arms of antidepressant trials show, while reporting the within-network difference against the psychedelic trials' own placebo arms as an association. It rests on one network meta-analysis whose list of MDMA trials is in an appendix not read here, hence single study. This is reader 43's half of the depression claim; reader 42's half rests on the open-label trial in major depressive disorder and its follow-up.

statement: As described second-hand in one historical narrative review (Passie, 2018), whose estimates rest on a sparse literature and on information given to the author, a few dozen therapists in the United States, most in California and elsewhere on the West Coast, used MDMA in psychotherapy from the late 1970s until it was scheduled in 1985, while it was neither an approved medicine nor a controlled substance. The caseloads reported come mostly from the practitioners' own accounts, among them more than 80 patients treated by Greer and Tolbert from 1980 to 1985. The outcome evidence the review describes consists of practitioners' reports, a 1984 exploratory survey of 16 therapists, an unpublished 1980 study in which nine people had one MDMA session each, and a follow-up of 29 of Greer and Tolbert's patients, which found no serious side effects. Two therapists had sexual contact with patients during MDMA sessions; both were sued and lost their licences. After the DEA recommended placing MDMA in Schedule I in July 1984, its administrative law judge concluded at the 1985 hearings that this was not required, and the DEA overruled the judge; the WHO's expert committee, when MDMA was scheduled internationally in late 1985, judged the therapeutic reports methodologically inadequate but urged research. Five applications to study MDMA submitted from 1986 to 1988 were put on clinical hold, and the first FDA-approved study of MDMA in humans, in healthy volunteers, began in 1992. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Before it was banned in 1985, a few dozen therapists in the United States used MDMA in talking therapy. Their reports were positive, but experts for the World Health Organization judged them not well enough designed to rely on, and two therapists had sex with patients during sessions. A US judge advised against the strictest ban, but the drug agency imposed it anyway. This history comes from one review based on old reports, memoirs and the author's own contacts.
population: Patients of psychotherapists in the United States who used MDMA before it was scheduled (late 1970s to 1985)
exposure: MDMA used in individual, couples and group psychotherapy
outcome: Extent and nature of therapeutic use; outcome evidence of the period; documented misconduct; scheduling sequence
magnitude: A few dozen therapists, 1977 or 1978 to 1985; reported caseloads: Zeff about 4000 people over 12 years (from a memoir), Greer and Tolbert more than 80 patients (1980 to 1985), Ingrasci 100 patients in about 150 sessions, Harlow more than 200 clients; outcome reports: Greer and Tolbert follow-up of 29 (23 with positive changes lasting 1 week to 2 years, no serious side effects), ARUPA survey 15 of 16 therapists positive; two therapists lost their licences after sexual contact with patients during sessions; DEA recommended Schedule I on 27 July 1984, its judge concluded against in 1985, overruled; five research applications on clinical hold (1986 to 1988); first FDA-approved human study 1992.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: From the relatively poor data in the literature and information given personally to the author, a few dozen therapists, most in California and elsewhere on the West Coast, used MDMA in psychotherapy between 1977 (title and abstract) or 1978 (Discussion) and 1985, when it was neither an FDA-approved drug nor a controlled substance; a physician could use it legally if self-synthesized, with informed consent and a peer-reviewed protocol.

evidence.locator: George Greer's work with MDMA in psychotherapy, 1st and 5th paragraphs; Leo Zeff—The Secret Chief, 2nd paragraph; Rick Ingrasci: MDMA in couples and patients with life-threatening illnesses, 1st paragraph; A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Greer, a psychiatrist, and Tolbert, a psychiatric nurse, treated more than 80 patients from 1980 to 1985; their published follow-up of 29 patients found no serious side effects or negative after-effects and 23 with positive changes lasting from 1 week to 2 years; Zeff gave MDMA to about 4000 people over 12 years (from a memoir); Ingrasci treated 100 patients in about 150 sessions, one-third with couples; Harlow treated more than 200 clients before 1985.

evidence.locator: A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Kueny's 1980 study, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: A 1984 exploratory survey of 16 therapists for ARUPA: 15 judged MDMA valuable in augmenting psychotherapy and all claimed complications were negligible; it was used as evidence at the hearings; an unpublished 1980 study gave one MDMA session to each of nine people.

evidence.locator: Physical abuse in MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Two therapists, Rick Ingrasci and Francesco DiLeo, initiated intimate body contact, sexual touch and intercourse with patients during MDMA sessions; both were sued and lost their licences; a Maryland appeals court (1991) upheld damages to DiLeo's patient, later diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety.

evidence.locator: Therapists opposed to the scheduling of MDMA in 1985, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th, 6th and 8th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The DEA recommended Schedule I on 27 July 1984; at the 1985 hearings its administrative law judge concluded that MDMA did not have to be placed in Schedule I; the DEA overruled the judge's decision; the WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, which scheduled MDMA internationally in late 1985, found the therapeutic reports intriguing but methodologically inadequate and urged research; five applications to study MDMA submitted from 1986 to 1988 were placed on clinical hold; after the FDA rejected a patient study and recommended a study in healthy volunteers, the first FDA-approved MDMA study in humans began in 1992.

risk_of_bias.note: One narrative review by a single author, relaying memoirs, interviews and proponents' documents without appraisal; the figures are second-hand.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive historical claim (starts low), resting only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3: stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand), rated down once because the review relays unappraised sources. It describes the period; it makes no claim that MDMA-assisted therapy worked or was safe then. The primary documents of 1986 on the list (Greer and Tolbert; Downing; Grinspoon and Bakalar) should replace these anchors when saved.
